newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worker compensation up 0.6 percent in quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worker compensation up 0.6 percent in quarter.

text.p: American workers' compensation gains slowed in the first three months of 1997 as slower-growing benefit costs moderated a pickup in wages and salaries, the Labour Department said on Tuesday.

Combined pay and benefits rose a smaller-than-expected 0.6 percent in the first quarter of the year, down from a 0.8 percent gain in the fourth quarter of 1996, the department said in its quarterly Employment Cost Index report.

The report cheered financial markets by giving traders one less reason to worry that labour costs will push up prices and prompt Federal Reserve policy-makers to further raise short-term interest rates to dampen the economy's vigour.

"It's a very positive sign," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Bank Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla. "It could be short-lived, but at least for the time being the (price) pressures from the labour side would still apppear to be moderate."

Wages and salaries, which represent about 70 percent of the index, jumped 0.9 percent in the first quarter, the largest gain in a year, after a 0.8 percent rise in the fourth quarter, the department said.
But benefit costs rose only a scant 0.1 percent, matching their smallest increase in a year, after a 0.7 percent gain in the fourth quarter, it said.

Economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisers, noting that benefit costs were held down by declines in manufacturing, said the mitigating impact of benefit costs on overall compensation may not last much longer.
"With the tightening labour markets and the pressure on firms to offer more benefits ... this clearly flies in the face of the anecdotal evidence that's been put out to investors," said Chan.

Benefit cost increases have slowed in recent years as employers shifted a greater share of health care costs onto their employees and opted for cheaper managed care plans. But many economists expect those costs to accelerate again, arguing that employers have already saved all that they can.

The Employment Cost Index, along with upcoming reports on the unemployment rate and gross domestic product, will be closely scrutinised by Fed policy-makers when they next consider their interest rate strategy May 20, Chan said.
"This report, I think, argues for complacency rather than for immediate urgency on the part of policy-makers," he said.
The Fed raised short-term interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month.
Economists noted that higher compensation for workers is not necessarily inflationary if the increases are matched by gains in productivity, which is difficult to measure with precision.
"My view is that the real gains in compensation are probably pretty close to the productivity gains that we've seen in the past year," said Barnett Bank's Reaser.
In the 12 months ended March 31, workers' total compensation rose 2.9 percent, compared with 2.9 percent in all of 1996 and 2.8 percent in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.
By comparison, the Consumer Price Index, which is widely believed to overstate inflation, though there is disagreement as to how much, rose 2.8 percent in the 12 months ended March 31.
Wages and salaries in the 12 months ended March 31 rose 3.3 percent, identical to the five-year-high increase of 1996, after a 3.1 percent gain in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.

Employers' cost of providing benefits, including medical insurance, rose 2 percent in the 12 months ended March 31, the same as for 1996, after a 1.8 percent gain in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.

Compensation for private industry workers in the first quarter rose 0.6 percent after climbing 0.7 percent in the fourth quarter, while state and local government workers' compensation rose 0.5 percent after a 0.8 percent rise in the fourth quarter.
